en-A2-0.b:
The past simple describes a finished action at a specific time in the past (yesterday, last week, in 2020, ago).

Regular verbs: add -ed: work → worked, play → played. Same form for all persons.

  • Ends in -e: add -d: live → lived
  • Consonant + y → -ied: study → studied
  • Short verb, one vowel + one consonant: double: stop → stopped, plan → planned

Questions and negatives use did / didn't + base verb: Did you work yesterday? I didn't work.

Pronunciation of -ed: [t] walked, [d] played, [ɪd] wanted, needed.

Common mistake: « Did you worked? » → Did you work?; « I didn't liked it » → I didn't like it.
en-A2-0.t:
Le prétérit (past simple) décrit une action terminée à un moment précis du passé (yesterday, last week, in 2020, ago). Il correspond souvent au passé composé français.

Verbes réguliers : ajoute -ed : work → worked, play → played. Même forme à toutes les personnes.

  • Finit par -e : ajoute -d : live → lived
  • Consonne + y → -ied : study → studied
  • Verbe court, une voyelle + une consonne : on double : stop → stopped, plan → planned

Questions et négations avec did / didn't + verbe de base : Did you work yesterday? I didn't work.

Prononciation de -ed : [t] walked, [d] played, [ɪd] wanted, needed.

Erreur fréquente : « Did you worked? » → Did you work? ; « I didn't liked it » → I didn't like it.
e: I worked late yesterday.
We visited Bruges last summer.
She studied French at university.
Did you watch the match?
They didn't call me.

en-A2-1.b:
Many common verbs are irregular in the past simple. You must learn them:

basepastbasepast
bewas / weregowent
havehaddodid
makemadesaysaid
getgotcomecame
seesawtaketook
knowknewthinkthought
buyboughtbringbrought
eatatedrinkdrank
writewrotespeakspoke
leaveleftfeelfelt

be: I/he/she/it was, you/we/they were. Questions/negatives: Were you…? I wasn't… (no did).

With did, use the base form: Did you go? I didn't see it.

Common mistake: « I goed », « I buyed » → I went, I bought.
en-A2-1.t:
Beaucoup de verbes courants sont irréguliers au prétérit. Il faut les apprendre :

baseprétéritbaseprétérit
be (être)was / werego (aller)went
have (avoir)haddo (faire)did
make (faire, fabriquer)madesay (dire)said
get (obtenir)gotcome (venir)came
see (voir)sawtake (prendre)took
know (savoir)knewthink (penser)thought
buy (acheter)boughtbring (apporter)brought
eat (manger)atedrink (boire)drank
write (écrire)wrotespeak (parler)spoke
leave (partir)leftfeel (ressentir)felt

be : I/he/she/it was, you/we/they were. Questions/négations : Were you…? I wasn't… (sans did).

Avec did, on utilise la base : Did you go? I didn't see it.

Erreur fréquente : « I goed », « I buyed » → I went, I bought.
e: I went to Brussels last weekend.
She bought a new phone.
We ate at a nice restaurant.
Were you at home yesterday?
I didn't see him.

en-A2-2.b:
The past continuous = was/were + verb-ing. It describes an action in progress at a moment in the past (like the French imparfait for ongoing actions).

  • At 8 pm, I was watching TV.
  • They were working all day.

Past continuous + past simple: a longer action interrupted by a short one: I was cooking when the phone rang.

while + continuous: While I was walking, it started to rain.

Negative / question: I wasn't sleeping. Were you listening?

State verbs (know, like, want, believe) are not usually used in the continuous: I knew him (not « was knowing »).

Common mistake: using the past continuous for every past description: When I was a child, I lived (or used to live) in Congo — not « was living » for long habits.
en-A2-2.t:
Le past continuous = was/were + verbe-ing. Il décrit une action en cours à un moment du passé (comme l'imparfait français pour une action en cours).

  • At 8 pm, I was watching TV. (À 20 h, je regardais la télé)
  • They were working all day.

Past continuous + past simple : une action longue interrompue par une action courte : I was cooking when the phone rang.

while (pendant que) + continu : While I was walking, it started to rain.

Négation / question : I wasn't sleeping. Were you listening?

Les verbes d'état (know, like, want, believe) ne s'emploient généralement pas au continu : I knew him (pas « was knowing »).

Erreur fréquente : utiliser le past continuous pour toute description au passé : When I was a child, I lived (ou used to live) in Congo — pas « was living » pour une longue habitude.
e: I was sleeping when you called.
What were you doing at 10 o'clock?
It was raining all morning.
While she was driving, she was listening to music.
We weren't working yesterday afternoon.
q: I was cooking when the phone ___ (ring)
___ I was walking, I met Tom.
I ___ him for years. (know, state verb)

en-A2-3.b:
Two common ways to talk about the future:

  • going to + verb: plans already decided, and predictions based on what you see: I'm going to study Dutch next year. Look at the clouds — it's going to rain.
  • will + verb: instant decisions, promises, offers, general predictions: The phone's ringing — I'll get it! I will call you. I think she'll win.

Negatives: I'm not going to…, I won't (will not)…

Also: present continuous for fixed arrangements: I'm meeting Sarah tomorrow.

After when, if, as soon as, use the present, not will: When I arrive, I'll call you.

Common mistake: « When I will arrive » → When I arrive; « I will to go » → I will go.
en-A2-3.t:
Deux façons courantes de parler du futur :

  • going to + verbe : projets déjà décidés, et prédictions basées sur ce qu'on voit : I'm going to study Dutch next year. Look at the clouds — it's going to rain.
  • will + verbe : décisions immédiates, promesses, offres, prédictions générales : The phone's ringing — I'll get it! I will call you. I think she'll win.

Négations : I'm not going to…, I won't (will not)…

Aussi : présent continu pour un rendez-vous fixé : I'm meeting Sarah tomorrow.

Après when, if, as soon as, on utilise le présent, pas will (contrairement au français « quand j'arriverai ») : When I arrive, I'll call you.

Erreur fréquente : « When I will arrive » → When I arrive ; « I will to go » → I will go.
e: I'm going to move to Ghent.
I'll help you with your bags.
It's going to snow tonight.
I won't tell anyone, I promise.
When I get home, I'll call you.
q: Plan: I ___ visit my aunt next week.
Instant decision: "It's cold." — "I ___ close the window."
When I ___ home, I'll call you.
Look at that sky! It ___ rain.

en-A2-4.b:
Comparatives compare two things; superlatives show the top of a group.

adjectivecomparativesuperlative
short (1 syllable)taller thanthe tallest
ending -yhappier thanthe happiest
long (2+ syllables)more expensive thanthe most expensive
  • Double consonant: big → bigger, hot → hottest.
  • Irregular: good → better → the best; bad → worse → the worst; far → further → the furthest.
  • Equality: as … as: She's as tall as me. · not as … as.
  • Less: less … than: less expensive than.

Common mistake: « more big », « more better », « bigger that » → bigger than, better.
en-A2-4.t:
Les comparatifs comparent deux choses ; les superlatifs indiquent le plus haut degré dans un groupe.

adjectifcomparatifsuperlatif
court (1 syllabe)taller thanthe tallest
terminé par -yhappier thanthe happiest
long (2+ syllabes)more expensive thanthe most expensive
  • Consonne doublée : big → bigger, hot → hottest.
  • Irréguliers : good → better → the best ; bad → worse → the worst ; far → further → the furthest.
  • Égalité : as … as : She's as tall as me. · not as … as.
  • Infériorité : less … than : less expensive than.

Erreur fréquente : « more big », « more better », « bigger that » → bigger than, better.
e: Antwerp is bigger than Ghent.
This is the best chocolate in Belgium.
Dutch is more difficult than English for me.
My brother is as tall as my father.
Today is hotter than yesterday.
q: Ghent is ___ city in Belgium? No — Brussels is. (big)

en-A2-5.b:
Adverbs of frequency say how often: always (100%), usually, often, sometimes, rarely / seldom, never (0%).

Position:

  • before the main verb: I always drink coffee. She never eats meat.
  • after the verb be: He is often late.
  • between auxiliary and verb: I have never been to Paris. You can always call me.
  • sometimes can also start the sentence: Sometimes I work from home.

Questions: How often do you…? — Once a week, twice a month, every day.

never is already negative: I never smoke (not « I don't never »).

Common mistake: « I drink always coffee » → I always drink coffee; « He always is late » → He is always late.
en-A2-5.t:
Les adverbes de fréquence indiquent combien de fois : always (toujours, 100 %), usually (d'habitude), often (souvent), sometimes (parfois), rarely / seldom (rarement), never (jamais, 0 %).

Place :

  • avant le verbe principal (contrairement au français !) : I always drink coffee. She never eats meat.
  • après le verbe be : He is often late.
  • entre l'auxiliaire et le verbe : I have never been to Paris. You can always call me.
  • sometimes peut aussi commencer la phrase : Sometimes I work from home.

Questions : How often do you…? — Once a week (une fois par semaine), twice a month, every day.

never est déjà négatif : I never smoke (pas « I don't never »).

Erreur fréquente : « I drink always coffee » → I always drink coffee ; « He always is late » → He is always late.
e: I usually get up at seven.
She is always on time.
We sometimes eat out on Fridays.
He never drinks alcohol.
How often do you go to the gym?
q: How ___ do you call your mother?

en-A2-6.b:
The present perfect = have/has + past participle. It links the past to the present.

  • Experience (in your life, no time given): I have visited London. Have you ever eaten sushi? I've never been to Spain.
  • Recent actions with just, already, yet: I've just finished. She has already left. Have you done it yet?
  • Result now: I've lost my keys (I don't have them now).

Past participle: regular = -ed; irregular: be → been, go → gone/been, do → done, see → seen, eat → eaten, write → written, take → taken.

been vs gone: He has been to Paris (and came back) / He has gone to Paris (he's there now).

Common mistake: « I have visited London last year » → I visited London last year (finished time → past simple).
en-A2-6.t:
Le present perfect = have/has + participe passé. Il relie le passé au présent.

  • Expérience (dans ta vie, sans date) : I have visited London. Have you ever eaten sushi? (As-tu déjà… ?) I've never been to Spain.
  • Actions récentes avec just, already, yet : I've just finished (je viens de finir). She has already left. Have you done it yet?
  • Résultat présent : I've lost my keys (je ne les ai pas maintenant).

Participe passé : régulier = -ed ; irrégulier : be → been, go → gone/been, do → done, see → seen, eat → eaten, write → written, take → taken.

been vs gone : He has been to Paris (il y est allé et revenu) / He has gone to Paris (il y est maintenant).

Erreur fréquente : « I have visited London last year » → I visited London last year (moment terminé → prétérit).
e: I have lived in Belgium for three years.
Have you ever been to Bruges?
She has just arrived.
I haven't finished my work yet.
We've already eaten.
q: He's ___ to the shop; he'll be back soon.

en-A2-7.b:
French uses the passé composé for both, but English separates them:

Past simplePresent perfect
finished time: yesterday, last year, in 2020, ago, when I was…unfinished or unspecified time: ever, never, already, yet, just, so far, today, this week
I saw him yesterday.I've seen him today.
She lived in Paris for 5 years (she doesn't anymore).She's lived in Ghent for 5 years (she still does).

Questions with When…? → past simple: When did you arrive?

A conversation often starts with the present perfect and continues with the past simple: Have you ever been to Italy? — Yes, I went there in 2018.

Common mistake: « When have you arrived? » → When did you arrive?
en-A2-7.t:
Le français utilise le passé composé pour les deux, mais l'anglais les distingue :

Past simplePresent perfect
moment terminé : yesterday, last year, in 2020, ago, when I was…période non terminée ou non précisée : ever, never, already, yet, just, so far, today, this week
I saw him yesterday.I've seen him today.
She lived in Paris for 5 years (elle n'y vit plus).She's lived in Ghent for 5 years (elle y vit toujours).

Questions avec When…? → prétérit : When did you arrive?

Une conversation commence souvent au present perfect et continue au prétérit : Have you ever been to Italy? — Yes, I went there in 2018.

Erreur fréquente : « When have you arrived? » → When did you arrive?
e: I've been to Italy. I went there in 2018.
When did you start learning Dutch?
I've lived here since 2022.
She worked in London from 2015 to 2019.
Have you seen my phone? I can't find it.
q: I ___ to Spain three times. (in my life)
Have you ever been to Rome? — Yes, I ___ there last year.

en-A2-8.b:
Use these words to talk about quantity:

  • many + plural countable: many books, many people
  • much + uncountable: much money, much time
  • a lot of / lots of + both (very common in positive sentences): a lot of friends, a lot of work

much and many are mainly used in questions and negatives: How much time? I don't have many friends. In positive sentences, a lot of sounds more natural: I have a lot of time (not « I have much time »).

Small quantities: a few + countable (a few days), a little + uncountable (a little sugar). Without a, it's negative: few people came (= almost nobody).

too much / too many = excessive: too much noise, too many cars.

Common mistake: « much people » → many people; « a few money » → a little money.
en-A2-8.t:
Ces mots expriment la quantité :

  • many + dénombrable pluriel : many books, many people
  • much + indénombrable : much money, much time
  • a lot of / lots of + les deux (très courant à l'affirmatif) : a lot of friends, a lot of work

much et many s'utilisent surtout dans les questions et négations : How much time? I don't have many friends. À l'affirmatif, a lot of est plus naturel : I have a lot of time (pas « I have much time »).

Petites quantités : a few + dénombrable (a few days, quelques jours), a little + indénombrable (a little sugar, un peu de sucre). Sans a, c'est négatif : few people came (= presque personne).

too much / too many = trop : too much noise, too many cars.

Erreur fréquente : « much people » → many people ; « a few money » → a little money.
e: How many languages do you speak?
I don't have much time today.
There are a lot of tourists in Bruges.
Can I have a little milk, please?
There are too many cars in the city.
q: I have ___ friends in Ghent. (positive, natural)

en-A2-9.b:
Obligation and advice:

  • must: strong obligation from the speaker, or rules (written): I must call my mother. You must wear a seatbelt.
  • have to: obligation from outside (rules, situation): I have to work on Saturday. She has to wear a uniform. Past: had to.
  • should: advice, opinion: You should see a doctor. You shouldn't smoke.

Negatives — careful!

  • mustn't = it's forbidden: You mustn't park here.
  • don't have to = it's not necessary: You don't have to come (you can if you want).

must and should: no -s, no to: He must go. But He has to go.

Common mistake: « You mustn't come » to mean « ce n'est pas obligatoire » → You don't have to come.
en-A2-9.t:
Obligation et conseil :

  • must : obligation forte venant de celui qui parle, ou règlement (écrit) : I must call my mother. You must wear a seatbelt.
  • have to : obligation extérieure (règles, situation) : I have to work on Saturday. She has to wear a uniform. Passé : had to.
  • should : conseil, opinion (devrais) : You should see a doctor. You shouldn't smoke.

Négations — attention !

  • mustn't = c'est interdit : You mustn't park here.
  • don't have to = ce n'est pas nécessaire : You don't have to come (tu peux si tu veux).

must et should : pas de -s, pas de to : He must go. Mais He has to go.

Erreur fréquente : « You mustn't come » pour dire « ce n'est pas obligatoire » → You don't have to come.
e: I have to get up early tomorrow.
You must show your ID card.
You should drink more water.
You mustn't smoke in the building.
You don't have to pay, it's free.
q: You ___ see this film, it's great! (advice)

en-A2-10.b:
Possessive pronouns replace possessive adjective + noun. They stand alone.

adjectivepronoun
my bookmine
your bookyours
his bookhis
her bookhers
our bookours
their booktheirs
  • Is this your phone? — Yes, it's mine.
  • Their house is bigger than ours.
  • a friend of mine (= un de mes amis).
  • Question: Whose …? Whose bag is this? — It's hers.

No apostrophe: yours, hers, ours, theirs (not « your's »).

Common mistake: « It's the mine » → It's mine; « a friend of me » → a friend of mine.
en-A2-10.t:
Les pronoms possessifs remplacent adjectif possessif + nom. Ils s'emploient seuls.

adjectifpronom
my bookmine (le mien)
your bookyours (le tien / le vôtre)
his bookhis (le sien, à lui)
her bookhers (le sien, à elle)
our bookours (le nôtre)
their booktheirs (le leur)
  • Is this your phone? — Yes, it's mine.
  • Their house is bigger than ours.
  • a friend of mine (= un de mes amis).
  • Question : Whose …? (à qui) Whose bag is this? — It's hers.

Pas d'apostrophe : yours, hers, ours, theirs (pas « your's »).

Erreur fréquente : « It's the mine » → It's mine (pas d'article) ; « a friend of me » → a friend of mine.
e: That's not my coat, mine is black.
Is this pen yours?
Whose keys are these? — They're his.
Our flat is smaller than theirs.
She's a good friend of mine.

en-A2-11.b:
After some verbs, use the -ing form (gerund); after others, use to + infinitive.

  • -ing after: enjoy, like, love, hate, finish, mind, avoid, stop, suggest, keep: I enjoy reading. She finished working. Do you mind waiting?
  • to + verb after: want, need, decide, hope, plan, learn, try, would like, promise, forget: I want to learn Dutch. We decided to move. I'd like to go.
  • After a preposition: always -ing: I'm interested in learning. Thanks for helping. Before leaving…
  • -ing as a subject: Swimming is good for you.

like / love / hate can take both: I like swimming / I like to swim. But would like → to.

Common mistake: « I enjoy to read » → I enjoy reading; « I want learn » → I want to learn; « I look forward to see you » → to seeing you.
en-A2-11.t:
Après certains verbes, on utilise la forme en -ing (gérondif) ; après d'autres, to + infinitif.

  • -ing après : enjoy (aimer), like, love, hate, finish, mind (déranger), avoid (éviter), stop, suggest, keep (continuer) : I enjoy reading. She finished working. Do you mind waiting?
  • to + verbe après : want, need, decide, hope, plan, learn, try, would like, promise, forget : I want to learn Dutch. We decided to move. I'd like to go.
  • Après une préposition : toujours -ing (le français met l'infinitif) : I'm interested in learning. Thanks for helping. Before leaving…
  • -ing comme sujet : Swimming is good for you. (Nager est bon pour toi)

like / love / hate acceptent les deux : I like swimming / I like to swim. Mais would like → to.

Erreur fréquente : « I enjoy to read » → I enjoy reading ; « I want learn » → I want to learn ; « I look forward to see you » → to seeing you.
e: I enjoy cooking for my friends.
I want to improve my English.
She decided to study medicine.
Thank you for coming.
Learning a language takes time.

en-A2-12.b:
The first conditional talks about a real, possible situation in the present or future and its result.

If + present simple, will + verb:

  • If it rains, I'll stay at home.
  • If you study, you'll pass the exam.
  • The order can change (no comma then): I'll call you if I have time.

Other possibilities in the result: imperative or modal: If you see Tom, tell him to call me. If you're tired, you can go home.

unless = if … not: I'll go unless it rains (= if it doesn't rain).

Same rule after when, as soon as, before, after: When I finish, I'll call you.

Common mistake: « If it will rain » → If it rains (never will after if here).
en-A2-12.t:
Le premier conditionnel parle d'une situation réelle, possible au présent ou au futur, et de son résultat.

If + présent simple, will + verbe :

  • If it rains, I'll stay at home. (S'il pleut, je resterai…)
  • If you study, you'll pass the exam.
  • L'ordre peut changer (alors sans virgule) : I'll call you if I have time.

Autres possibilités dans le résultat : impératif ou modal : If you see Tom, tell him to call me. If you're tired, you can go home.

unless = if … not (à moins que) : I'll go unless it rains (= s'il ne pleut pas).

Même règle après when, as soon as, before, after : When I finish, I'll call you.

Erreur fréquente : « If it will rain » → If it rains (jamais will après if ici).
e: If it's sunny tomorrow, we'll go to the beach.
If you need help, call me.
I'll come unless I'm too tired.
If you don't hurry, you'll miss the train.
When I get the results, I'll tell you.
q: I'll call you if I ___ time.
If you see her, ___ her hello.
I'll go ___ it rains. (= if it doesn't rain)
If you don't hurry, you ___ the bus.
If she ___ late, we'll start without her.
